summary.text: Babylon was an ancient city on the lower Euphrates in southern Mesopotamia, in modern-day Iraq, about 85 kilometres south of Baghdad.
It was the main cultural and political centre of Babylonia, and its rulers established two important empires, the Old Babylonian and the Neo-Babylonian.
Its Hanging Gardens and Walls were ranked among the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World, though some scholars question whether the gardens were real.

facts.label: Location
facts.value: Lower Euphrates, about 85 km south of Baghdad

facts.label: Neo-Babylonian capital
facts.value: Babylon was its capital from 626 to 539 BC

facts.label: Population milestone
facts.value: Perhaps the first city above 200,000 people

items.prompt: Babylon began as a small town in the Akkadian Empire. Which king built it into a major city and declared himself its king?

options.label: Shar-Kali-Sharri of Akkad
Cyrus the Great of Persia
Samsu-iluna, Hammurabi's son
Hammurabi, an Amorite king

items.explain: Hammurabi founded the Old Babylonian Empire, built Babylon into a major city and declared himself its king.

items.prompt: Many guides say Babylon's name means 'gate of the god(s)'. How do scholars increasingly view that reading?

options.label: As a folk etymology for an older, unknown name
As the proven original Sumerian name of the city
As a Greek invention made up in Herodotus's day
As an Egyptian name that was borrowed later

items.explain: The 'gate of god' reading is increasingly viewed as a Semitic folk etymology explaining an unknown original non-Semitic place name.

items.prompt: A guide presents the Hanging Gardens as certain history. Why do some scholars doubt they were real?

options.label: They are named in every Babylonian text found
They were built only after Alexander's conquest
No surviving Babylonian text mentions them
They were built under Hammurabi, too early to fit

items.explain: They are not mentioned in any extant Babylonian text, so some scholars question their historical reality.

items.prompt: The Neo-Babylonian Empire fell in 539 BC. What happened to the city of Babylon next?

options.label: It was abandoned at once and forgotten
It came under a series of later empires
It stayed independent for centuries
It was moved to the Persian Gulf

items.explain: The city came under Achaemenid, Seleucid, Parthian, Roman, Sassanid and Muslim rule, with its last known habitation in the 11th century AD.

items.prompt: Despite its heritage status, what is putting Babylon's ruins at risk today?

options.label: Rapid local construction near the ruins
Floods from the Euphrates each spring
Heavy crowds of foreign tourists
Mining of clay for brick making

items.explain: Local construction is rapidly increasing and threatens to encroach on the ruins; the few visitors are almost all Iraqis.

items.prompt: After the Assyrians destroyed and then rebuilt Babylon, it became the capital of which short-lived empire?

options.label: The Old Babylonian Empire
The Achaemenid Empire
The Neo-Babylonian Empire
The Akkadian Empire

items.explain: After the Assyrians destroyed and rebuilt it, Babylon became the capital of the short-lived Neo-Babylonian Empire, from 626 to 539 BC.
